conditions.name: Evidence appraisal and measures of association
conditions.overview: Exam study of risk comparisons and threats to interpretation. Worked numbers and study scenarios are fictional, not treatment-effect estimates.

sources.title: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 3, Section 5 — Measures of Association
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.edition: Third edition; archived page last reviewed May 18, 2012
sources.locator: Risk ratio: definition and method for calculating risk ratio
sources.limitations: Archived official educational reference for stable statistical definitions; not a current clinical guideline. All example numbers here are original.

sources.title: Biases to Consider in Vaccine Effectiveness Studies
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.limitations: Definitions are applied to an original hypothetical study, not a claim about any vaccine or treatment.

sections.title: Relative risk
sections.text: A risk ratio divides event risk in the group of interest by event risk in the comparison group. One indicates equal observed risks; values below one indicate lower observed risk.

sections.title: Original worked comparison
sections.text: In a fictional study, 10 events among 200 participants versus 20 among 200 gives risks of 5% and 10%, and a risk ratio of 0.50. These invented counts describe association.

sections.title: Interpret association cautiously
sections.text: Observational comparisons may be distorted by confounding, selection bias or differences in information collection. A factor associated with both exposure and outcome can confound their measured relationship.

questions.stem: An invented cohort study records an event in 10 of 200 people with exposure X and 20 of 200 without X. Which risk ratio compares the exposed group with the unexposed group?
questions.explanation: The risks are 10/200 and 20/200. Dividing 0.05 by 0.10 gives 0.50.

distractorExplanations.C: One would indicate equal observed risks.
distractorExplanations.E: Ten is an event count, not this ratio.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate risk ratio from two fictional event risks.

questions.stem: In a fictional observational study, exposure X is associated with hospital admission. Older age is more common among people with X and independently increases admission risk. Which issue most directly threatens the unadjusted association?

choices.text: A perfectly randomized exposure
A guaranteed causal effect of X
Specificity of an unrelated test
Confounding by age
Absence of any possible bias

questions.explanation: Age is associated with both exposure and outcome; it can distort the observed exposure-outcome relationship.

distractorExplanations.A: The study is observational, not randomized.
distractorExplanations.B: Association alone does not establish that claim.
distractorExplanations.C: Test specificity does not address this imbalance.
distractorExplanations.E: The described imbalance supplies a potential bias.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a potential confounder in an observational comparison.

conditions.name: Diagnostic test interpretation
conditions.overview: Exam study of test-result denominators and population context using fictional counts; no patient-specific diagnostic interpretation.

sources.title: Epidemiology Glossary
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

sources.title: Optimizing Epidemiology–Laboratory Collaborations
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.edition: CDC Field Epidemiology Manual web chapter; displayed edition not specified
sources.locator: Interpreting Laboratory Results: sensitivity, specificity, prevalence and source population
sources.limitations: Official epidemiology teaching reference; no condition-specific testing recommendation is asserted.

sections.title: Choose the correct denominator
sections.text: Sensitivity concerns people with disease; specificity concerns people without disease. Positive predictive value concerns people with a positive result: what fraction truly have the condition?

sections.title: Original predictive-value example
sections.text: If a fictional dataset has 90 true-positive and 90 false-positive results, its positive predictive value is 90/(90+90), or 50%. The denominator includes all positive results.

sections.title: Apply population context
sections.text: Interpretation considers sensitivity, specificity and disease prevalence. Check whether the population used to estimate test characteristics differs from the population being tested.

questions.stem: A fictional test dataset contains 90 true-positive, 90 false-positive, 10 false-negative and 810 true-negative results. What is the positive predictive value?
questions.explanation: There are 180 positive results, of which 90 are true positives: 90/180 equals 50%.
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish positive predictive value from sensitivity using original counts.

questions.stem: A fictional test was evaluated in one population and is now discussed for a population with different disease prevalence. What is the most appropriate interpretive consideration?

choices.text: Ignore the populations once a result is positive
Assume every positive result establishes disease
Use specificity alone to infer predictive value
Assume the original predictive value transfers unchanged
Consider prevalence and differences between the two populations

questions.explanation: CDC identifies prevalence and the population used to estimate test characteristics as important interpretive considerations.

distractorExplanations.B: A positive result can be false positive.
distractorExplanations.C: One characteristic alone omits relevant context.
distractorExplanations.D: Different populations require reassessment of context.

questions.learningObjective: Identify population context when interpreting diagnostic-test performance.

conditions.name: Shared decision making
conditions.overview: Study collaborative decision making in fictional exam encounters; this module supplies communication concepts, not a treatment recommendation.

sources.title: About Shared Decision Making
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality

sources.title: The SHARE Approach Essential Steps of Shared Decision Making
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality

sections.title: Evidence and values
sections.text: Shared decision making combines evidence with the person’s goals, values, preferences and circumstances. Understanding trade-offs and what matters to the person is central.

sections.title: Discuss options
sections.text: SHARE begins by inviting participation, then comparing benefits and harms and eliciting preferences before reaching a decision together.

sections.title: Revisit the decision
sections.text: The SHARE process includes follow-up: revisit the decision and assess how implementation is going, rather than treating a choice as permanently settled.

questions.stem: In a fictional exam encounter, two evidence-supported options offer different burdens and benefits. The person understands the options but has not explained which outcomes matter most. Which next step best supports shared decision making?

choices.text: Choose the option preferred by the clinician
Ask a relative to decide without participation
Explore the person’s goals and preferences
Treat the decision aid as the final decision
Avoid discussing trade-offs

questions.explanation: An informed comparison must be connected to the person’s own goals, preferences and circumstances.

distractorExplanations.A: Clinician preference alone omits the person’s values.
distractorExplanations.D: A tool supports dialogue; it does not replace it.
distractorExplanations.E: Trade-offs are part of informed collaboration.

questions.learningObjective: Integrate values and evidence in a preference-sensitive exam scenario.

questions.stem: A fictional exam patient and clinician select an option after reviewing its benefits, harms and personal fit. Which action completes the follow-through emphasized in AHRQ’s SHARE process?

choices.text: Declare that the choice can never be reconsidered
Arrange to revisit the decision and its implementation
Stop asking about the person’s preferences
Promise that the selected option has no harms
Repeat only the clinician’s preferred option

questions.explanation: SHARE includes evaluating the decision, with a plan to revisit it and monitor implementation.

distractorExplanations.A: A decision may need to be revisited.
distractorExplanations.E: Follow-through is broader than repeating one option.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize follow-up as part of shared decision making.

conditions.name: Health literacy and clear communication
conditions.overview: Study communication and comprehension in fictional vignettes. Universal precautions apply to communication, not to a claim of clinical safety from this app.

sources.title: Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, 3rd Edition: Introduction
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.edition: Third edition; page last reviewed February 2024
sources.locator: What Are Health Literacy Universal Precautions?; Why Use Health Literacy Universal Precautions?

sources.title: Communicate Clearly: Tool 4
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.edition: Third edition; page last reviewed April 2024
sources.locator: Actions: clear spoken communication and confirming understanding

sections.title: Use universal precautions
sections.text: Difficulty understanding health information cannot reliably be inferred from appearance or education. AHRQ recommends making communication understandable and confirming comprehension with everyone.

sections.title: Plain language
sections.text: Use familiar words, a clear pace and a limited set of important points. Replace jargon and vague descriptions with concrete explanations.

sections.title: Confirm understanding
sections.text: Ask the person to explain important information in their own words. This gives more information about understanding than a yes-or-no question about whether everything is clear.

questions.stem: In a fictional exam vignette, a university professor seems comfortable discussing a complex plan. Which communication approach best follows health literacy universal precautions?

choices.text: Skip comprehension checks because of education
Use more technical terms to demonstrate expertise
Reserve clear explanations for people who fail a literacy test
Use understandable explanations and confirm comprehension
Assume professional status guarantees comprehension

questions.explanation: Universal precautions simplify communication and confirm understanding for everyone, because difficulty can occur in any person.

distractorExplanations.B: Extra jargon does not support understanding.
distractorExplanations.C: Universal precautions are not reserved for a subgroup.

questions.learningObjective: Apply universal precautions without relying on educational status.

questions.stem: In a fictional teaching encounter, an explanation has been given using familiar language. Which question best checks understanding?

choices.text: How would you describe the main steps in your own words?
You understand everything, correct?
Could you repeat each technical term exactly?
Can we assume the handout answered everything?
Would you agree that the explanation was simple?

questions.explanation: Asking for an explanation in the person’s own words helps confirm understanding of the important information.

distractorExplanations.B: A yes-or-no response provides limited evidence.
distractorExplanations.C: Repeating terms does not demonstrate the main meaning.
distractorExplanations.D: A handout alone does not confirm comprehension.
distractorExplanations.E: Perceived simplicity does not demonstrate understanding.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an open comprehension check from reassurance-seeking questions.

conditions.name: Quality improvement and systems safety
conditions.overview: Study improvement methods and systems thinking through invented exam scenarios. The app does not provide a clinical incident-management service.

sources.title: Plan-Do-Study-Act Worksheet, Directions, and Examples
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.edition: Third edition; page last reviewed March 2024
sources.locator: PDSA directions; Plan, Do, Study and Act

sources.title: Types of Health Care Quality Measures
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.locator: Structural Measures; Process Measures; Outcome Measures

sources.title: System-Focused Event Investigation and Analysis Guide
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.edition: CANDOR Toolkit; page last reviewed August 2022
sources.locator: A Systems Approach; follow-up and measurement

sections.title: Test and learn
sections.text: PDSA plans a small change and a measurement, tries it, studies the results, then adapts or expands based on learning. Small, brief tests can precede broader implementation.

sections.title: Differentiate measures
sections.text: Structure describes capacity or systems; process describes what is done; outcome describes effects on health. Outcomes can reflect factors beyond an individual provider’s control.

sections.title: Identify system factors
sections.text: Safety-event investigation examines contributing processes, technology and working conditions. Its prevention goal requires addressing system vulnerabilities and measuring whether changes work.

questions.stem: In a fictional improvement exercise, a team wants to test a new reminder. Which initial plan best follows the PDSA method?

choices.text: Deploy everywhere without defining an outcome
Decide success only from enthusiasm
Avoid observing workflow during the test
Promise the first design will never change
Test a small change, define a measure and time frame, then review results

questions.explanation: A small, measurable test supports learning before adaptation or broader implementation.

distractorExplanations.A: This removes the opportunity for a defined small test.
distractorExplanations.B: Enthusiasm alone does not assess the planned result.
distractorExplanations.C: Observations inform learning during the test.
distractorExplanations.D: Iteration is part of the method.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a small, measurable improvement test in an exam scenario.

questions.stem: In a fictional safety vignette, several staff members have nearly selected the wrong item from the same confusing electronic menu. Which response best addresses recurrence from a systems perspective?

choices.text: Label only the latest staff member as careless
Declare safety assured because no harm occurred
Investigate the interface and workflow, redesign contributing hazards and evaluate the change
Require everyone to memorize the current menu permanently
Suppress reports to improve the safety statistics

questions.explanation: A recurring interface hazard calls for investigation of contributing system factors and evaluation of corrective changes.

distractorExplanations.A: Individual blame alone leaves the recurring hazard.
distractorExplanations.B: A near miss can reveal a vulnerability.
distractorExplanations.D: Memorization alone leaves the confusing design.
distractorExplanations.E: Suppressing reports hides opportunities for prevention.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a systems response to a recurring fictional safety hazard.

conditions.name: Social needs, equity and resource connections
conditions.overview: Study social context and respectful support in fictional board vignettes. No real person’s social or health records are needed.

sources.title: About SDOH in Healthcare
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality

sources.title: Attend to Social Needs: Tool 18
sources.organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
sources.edition: Third edition; page last reviewed April 2024
sources.locator: Assess social needs and support systems; connect with resources; follow up

sections.title: Community context and individual needs
sections.text: Community conditions include transportation, food availability and access to services. People in the same community can have different individual social needs, such as food insecurity or financial strain.

sections.title: Ask respectfully
sections.text: Explain why social questions are being asked and how information will be used. Discuss needs privately, ask what help is wanted and obtain permission before sharing with support contacts.

sections.title: Close the referral loop
sections.text: Support connections to appropriate community resources, help with access barriers and follow up to determine whether a requested referral was completed. Keep resource information current.

questions.stem: In a fictional exam scenario, two people live in the same neighborhood. One cannot afford food while the other has stable food access. Which statement best distinguishes social determinants from individual social needs?

choices.text: Neighborhood residence makes their individual needs identical
Shared community conditions can coexist with different individual social needs
Food insecurity is unrelated to social context
A person’s social needs are determined solely by diagnosis
Community information replaces asking about individual circumstances

questions.explanation: AHRQ distinguishes community-level conditions from individuals’ differing social needs within that community.

distractorExplanations.A: Shared location does not make needs identical.
distractorExplanations.C: Food insecurity is a listed social need.
distractorExplanations.D: Diagnosis alone does not describe social needs.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish shared community conditions from differing individual social needs.

questions.stem: In a fictional exam encounter, a person requests transportation help and agrees to a resource referral. Which next action best completes the support process?

choices.text: Give an old number and assume access succeeded
Contact every relative without permission
Record the referral and never check its result
Confirm the resource connection and address barriers if it was not completed
Treat a positive social-needs screen as refusal of all care

questions.explanation: AHRQ recommends following up to learn whether a referral was completed and documenting its outcome.

distractorExplanations.A: An unverified connection may leave the need unmet.
distractorExplanations.C: Referral placement alone does not establish completion.
distractorExplanations.E: A social need is not a refusal of care.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize follow-through after a requested fictional resource referral.
